\chapter{Places}
\label{ch:ml-places}
\hlchaptermodality{105}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a country, a town, a city and a capital, and say what kind of place Kerala and India are.}

From cold: the scale of places, and the one word on it that does not sort by size.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rājyaṁ]{\ml{രാജ്യം} — a country}

\label{lesson:ML-C105-raajyam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}}. Say \textbf{\ml{കേരളം}}. Then say \textbf{\ml{നാട്}} — the word that can stretch from a home region all the way up to a country.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}} (\emph{rājyaṁ}) — \textbf{a country}.

\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} is one. \textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} is not — it is a part of one.

\textbf{\ml{നാട്}} could not tell you that. It covers a home region, a district or a country, and the situation decides which — so it can name the thing without fixing its size. \textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}} fixes it. That is the whole of what this word adds.

\begin{culture}
The Sanskrit behind it means \textbf{a realm}, and it is built on the word for a \textbf{king}. What the word names is \textbf{kingship} — rule as an institution — not the land, the people or the borders.

\textbf{It ends in -\ml{ം}}, which by now tells you what it will do when a case ending arrives.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rājyaṁ}
  \item \emph{nāṭŭ}, then \emph{rājyaṁ} — the word that floats, then the one that does not
  \item what the Sanskrit behind it is built on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A country? (\textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}}.) What could \textbf{\ml{നാട്}} not do that this word does? (\textbf{Fix the size} — \ml{നാട്} floats.) What is the word built on? (\textbf{The word for a king}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nagaraṁ]{\ml{നഗരം} — a city}

\label{lesson:ML-C105-nagaram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a country}. Then say the word you were given for a settled place somebody is from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} (\emph{nagaraṁ}) — \textbf{a city}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}} & \emph{rājyaṁ} & a country \\
\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} & \emph{nagaraṁ} & a city \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} & \emph{ūrŭ} & a town, a settled place — \textbf{yours already} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{These two are not a big one and a small one}, and it is worth saying so rather than teaching you a rule that Malayalam does not keep.

\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} is the word in ordinary modern use. It is what a newspaper prints and what a speaker reaches for when naming a city. \textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} is \textbf{older}, and its own lesson told you where it mostly lives now: \textbf{buried in place-names the length of the south}, and in talk of the settled place somebody is \emph{from}.

So the difference is not a line on a map. \textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} is what you say about a city today; \textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} is the old word, still alive in names and in speaking of where somebody belongs.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nagaraṁ}
  \item the three in order — \emph{rājyaṁ}, \emph{nagaraṁ}, \emph{ūrŭ}
  \item which of the two is the word in ordinary use today, and where the other one mostly survives
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A city? (\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}}.) Which of the two is the word in ordinary use today? (\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}}.) Where does \textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} mostly survive? (\textbf{In place-names}, and in speaking of where somebody is from.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[talasthānaṁ]{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം} — a capital}

\label{lesson:ML-C105-thalasthaanam}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a city}. Then say the word for the part of your body that sits on top.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}} (\emph{talasthānaṁ}) — \textbf{a capital}.

\textbf{It opens with a word you already have.} The head you learned among the body parts, \textbf{\ml{തല}} — this book wrote it \emph{thala} there and writes it \emph{ta-} here, which is the same word and two spellings of the same first letter. The second half, \emph{sthānaṁ}, is a \textbf{place}, and it is given in sound only because this book has not taught it as a word of its own.

A capital is a \textbf{head-place}.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{English says exactly the same thing, and hides it.} \emph{Capital} comes from Latin \emph{caput} — \textbf{head}. Two languages, two roots, one idea: the city at the top of the body.

Malayalam keeps the head visible. \textbf{\ml{തല}} is right there at the front of the word every time you say it; an English speaker has to be told.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{talasthānaṁ}, slowly — the head, then \emph{sthānaṁ}
  \item the body part hiding at the front of it
  \item \emph{nagaraṁ}, then \emph{talasthānaṁ} — a city, then the head one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A capital? (\textbf{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}}.) What are its two halves? (\textbf{\ml{തല}}, the \textbf{head}, and \emph{sthānaṁ}, a \textbf{place}.) What does the English word hide that the Malayalam one shows? (\textbf{The same head} — Latin \emph{caput}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rājyaṁ enna ōrmma]{(country, city, capital) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R105-places-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{country}, \emph{city} and \emph{capital}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a scale, and one word that is not on it}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}} & \emph{rājyaṁ} & a country \\
\textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} & \emph{nagaraṁ} & a city \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} & \emph{ūrŭ} & a town, a settled place — yours long before this chapter \\
\textbf{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}} & \emph{talasthānaṁ} & a capital \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The last one is not a size at all.} A capital is a city picked out by what happens in it, and it can be large or small.

\textbf{And the middle two are not a clean pair of sizes either} — you were told that \textbf{\ml{നഗരം}} is the word in ordinary use for a city today, while \textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} is the older one, surviving in place-names and in speaking of where somebody is from. Only \textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}} sits unambiguously at the top.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could name the places before you could say what kind of thing they were.} \textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} have been yours for a long while. \textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} gave you the settled end of the scale, and \textbf{\ml{നാട്}} gave you a word that floats over everything from a home region to a country. What was missing was a word that does \textbf{not} float, the ordinary modern word for a city, and the capital.

And one of the four was half-built already: \textbf{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}} opens with \emph{tala}, the \textbf{head} you learned among the body parts. The word was waiting on a piece you had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rājyaṁ}, \emph{nagaraṁ}, \emph{ūrŭ}, \emph{talasthānaṁ}
  \item which one is picked out by what happens in it, not by its size
  \item which one is the old word that survives in place-names
  \item \emph{indya}, then what kind of thing it is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Country, city, capital? (\textbf{\ml{രാജ്യം}, \ml{നഗരം}, \ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}}.) Which one is picked out by what happens in it? (\textbf{\ml{തലസ്ഥാനം}}.) What is hiding at the front of it? (\textbf{\ml{തല}}, the \textbf{head}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
